sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for Gilbertese: Blevins & Harrison 1999 'Trimoraic feet in Gilbertese' (OL 38(2): 203-230), the catalog's deciding primary. It remains paywalled and unreachable by any open route (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/S2 closed, MUSE captcha, no repository copy, no search-engine hit; The sweep did, however, read two open first-hand texts newly fetched sources from archive.org: Bingham 1908's dictionary (p. viii, Note 5: accent weakly marked, final syllable as a rule unaccented, two equal accents in long compounds), which refines and supports the catalog's hedged right-edge/non-final coding without superseding B&H, and Trussel 1979's Peace Corps Grammar Handbook (previously an unfetched wishlist item), which is silent on stress. Catalog coding unchanged; all files and probes.

new_statements.quote: Note 5. In very many words the accent is not very marked. As a rule, the final syllable is not accented. There are exceptions, numbers of which are marked in the dictionary. Many long words have two accents about equal in force, especially compound words.
new_statements.citation: Bingham, Hiram. 1908. A Gilbertese-English dictionary. Boston: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions.
new_statements.locator: Key to the Pronunciation, Note 5, printed p. viii (pdf p. 12; scanned text l. 342-346)
new_statements.reading: A first-hand, pre-1999 statement that Gilbertese accent is weak and non-final with multiple roughly equal accents in long words. It is consistent with the catalog's right-edge, non-final, iterating analysis (B&H's penultimate-mora loudness peak in every trimoraic foot) and independently supports the QS-HEDGED coding (accent 'not very marked', cf. Groves 1985 'much more even'), but it gives no syllable/mora-counting rule and was written by a missionary lexicographer, not a phonologist.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: every quoted fragment is verbatim at the stated page in the held carriers (Martinez-Paricio 2013: 249 and fn. 2; Martinez-Paricio & Kager 2021: 49; Groves et al. 1985: 18 sec. 2.6). (2) The classification rests on the right work -- Blevins & Harrison 1999 is the only dedicated analysis of Gilbertese stress and nothing newer or instrumental was found (secondaries through 2021 cite only it and state no acoustic measurements exist) -- but we do not hold it; the rule reaches us through three mutually consistent secondary quotations, so the grade 'carried-quote' and the QS-HEDGED verdict are honest. The hedge is warranted independently (B&H call their contours impressionistic; Groves 1985 reports near-even stress; Golston 2021 reanalyses as pitch accent). (3) Nothing seen suggests the coding (right-edge, mora-counting penultimate-mora stress iterating in trimoraic feet

sources.citation: Bingham, Hiram. 1908. A Gilbertese-English dictionary. Boston: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Key to the Pronunciation, pp. vii-viii.
sources.quote: Note 5. In very many words the accent is not very marked. As a rule, the final syllable is not accented. There are exceptions, numbers of which are marked in the dictionary. Many long words have two accents about equal in force, especially compound words.
sources.locator: Key to the Pronunciation, Note 5, printed p. viii (pdf p. 12)
sources.note: First-hand, pre-Blevins & Harrison observation by the missionary lexicographer: accent is weakly marked, the final syllable is as a rule unaccented (exceptions are marked in the dictionary with an acute after the accented vowel, e.g. U'ti 'louse', A'ai 'four', Kakao'mara), and long/compound words carry two roughly equal accents. No syllable- or mora-counting rule is stated.
